subject: Accounting
title: Fixed vs. Variable Costs
description: A fast breakdown of Fixed vs. Variable Costs for builders.

hook.text: A gym pays $10,000 rent whether one person works out or a thousand. That's a fixed cost.

buildup.text: Fixed costs don't change with production volume—rent, salaries, insurance stay constant.

discovery.text: Variable costs rise and fall with output—raw materials, packaging, sales commissions.

twist.text: A business with high fixed costs needs lots of sales to break even—but profits soar after that point.

climax.text: Understanding cost structure helps managers predict how profits change as sales fluctuate.

punchline.text: Fixed costs wait. Variable costs follow every sale.

quiz.question: What is a fixed cost?
options: A cost that stays the same regardless of production volume
A cost that changes with each unit produced

details.summary: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of production volume; variable costs change proportionally with output. This topic explains cost behavior patterns, mixed costs, and why understanding the distinction is essential for budgeting and decision-making.
details.whyItMatters: Managers who don't understand cost behavior make poor predictions. Knowing which costs change with volume and which don't is the foundation of budgeting, pricing, and break-even analysis.
takeaways: Fixed costs like rent and salaries stay the same whether you produce one unit or one million
Variable costs like raw materials and direct labor increase in proportion to units produced
Per-unit fixed costs decrease as volume rises, creating economies of scale

faq.question: What are fixed and variable costs?
faq.answer: Fixed costs remain the same regardless of how many units are produced—like rent or insurance premiums. Variable costs change in direct proportion to production volume—like raw materials or sales commissions. Understanding this distinction is fundamental to cost management.

faq.question: Why do fixed costs per unit decrease as volume increases?
faq.answer: Because the same total fixed cost is spread over more units. If rent is $10,000/month and you produce 1,000 units, rent per unit is $10. At 10,000 units, it drops to $1 per unit. This is the core mechanism behind economies of scale.
